# English in Sweden: Functions, features and debates

## Abstract

English has for a long time had a strong position in the Swedish sociolinguistic context. English is ubiquitous in the contemporary Swedish public sphere, and good knowledge of English can be found in all sections of society. Far from only being used as a lingua franca for international communication, English is today also pervasively used in domains of business, higher education and academia, as well as in the media and for entertainment purposes. This growing presence of English in Sweden has led to language debates about the status and the role of English in Sweden and concerns of whether English is a threat to Swedish. This article discusses the status and the manifold functions of English in Sweden and describes the uses and features of English in the Swedish context. It concludes with a discussion of the current debates on the uses and the role of English in Sweden.

## INTRODUCTION

Knowledge of foreign languages has so far been reserved for the very few, the so-called educated. If a foreign language-and the choice would then reasonably fall on English-were to be introduced as a mandatory subject in compulsory school, an old educational gap would thereby at least be somewhat bridged. A window to the world would open to the broad mass of citizens. (SOU, 1948, p. 7, translation) In the 1940s, the Swedish School Commission proposed new guidelines for the teaching of foreign languages. In that report, the teaching of English, a language which until then had not been widely taught, was considered 'a tool for democratisation' (Cabau-Lampa, 2007, p. 337) . Through the teaching of English, Swedish citizens' view of the world and economic opportunities would be expanded. Today, there is no need to make such an argument for the teaching and learning of English, as English is ubiquitous in Sweden and its presence is felt in many areas of society, from education and work to entertainment. Instead, knowledge of English is today assumed to be a necessary skill.

When considering English in the world, in Kachru's (1985) Three Circles model, Sweden and its Nordic neighbours are classified as countries in the Expanding Circle. However, societal use and knowledge of English in Sweden is so high that the main subject of debate in Sweden since the 1990s has been whether English is transitioning from a foreign language to a second language (McArthur, 1996; Modiano, 2003 Modiano, , 2017;; Phillipson, 1992; Viberg, 2000) . Concurrently,

debates to what extent English, once considered a tool for democratisation, could be contributing to linguistic inequalities have also arisen. In the span of five decades, the debates surrounding English in Sweden developed from viewing English as a positive force to something more critically discussed. This article provides a current perspective on English in Sweden and discusses the current domains where English use is frequent, its functions and features, as well as current linguistic debates. Svartengren (1948) almost 80 years ago identified that already at that time English was becoming more prominent not only in the academic lives of scientists, but also everyday lives of Swedes: 'But why did the errand-boy, the shopgirl and the clerk suddenly want English? With these, the language followed the dollar and the pound, the banana, the coal, the tourist, and above all, the cinema' (p. 154). With English came economic opportunities, tourism and entertainment.

## THE DOMAINS AND FUNCTIONS OF ENGLISH IN SWEDEN

Perhaps not unexpectedly, that is true today as well. English, however, is not only used by scientists and in domains where hospitality would be a necessary ingredient; English today has a variety of functions, which span the areas of everyday and working life of most Swedes. It is this wide use that has prompted the debates of whether English is a foreign or second language. Below, we will turn to a discussion of to what extent this wide use is truly all-encompassing or perhaps limited only to certain contexts, circumstances or functions.

## English in leisure

As in many places around the world, in Sweden, English is very often used for entertainment or leisure purposes. Past surveys of uses of a foreign language (which for most Swedes can be assumed to be English) have shown that a large majority of Swedes regularly use English not only for watching television and movies and using the Internet (Eurobarometer, 2012) , but also for leisure reading (Eurobarometer, 2012; Mežek, 2013) . The import and sale of books in English has been increasing, so much so that in 2022, for example, over 3.8 million books in English were sold in Sweden, almost half of them non-fiction books (SBF & SFF, 2023) . English is also used for informational purposes, for example, when using the Internet and watching transnational news, which about a quarter of Swedes do frequently (Widholm, 2019) .

While these kinds of uses of English are mostly receptive, some Swedes also use English productively: some communicate with friends in English (Bolton & Meierkord, 2013; Eurobarometer, 2012) and use English on the social media (Laitinen et al., 2017) . These kinds of uses of English are presumably more common for younger generations, as they spend more time on the Internet in general (Internetstiftelsen, 2022) , are more likely to use streaming services to watch content and listen to podcasts (Facht & Ohlsson, 2021) and also play digital games (Olsson, 2012; Sundqvist & Sylvén, 2014) . Even many of the youngest Swedes today come in contact with English daily: on average, Swedish kindergartners and first grades spend more than 7 h a week watching videos, listening to music and playing games in English, although the differences between individuals can be great (Sylvén, 2022) . Since English plays a big role in young people's lives, the mixing of English and Swedish is quite common as well (Sharp, 2007) .

## THE DOMAINS AND FUNCTIONS OF ENGLISH IN SWEDEN
### Discipline

English in the private lives of Swedes is therefore commonly used for entertainment, information and leisure purposes, and mostly receptively. These kinds of uses, although surveyed, have not been subject to that much critical discussion, presumably because they are to be expected, especially considering the spread of Anglophone, and in particular American, media. They also do not constitute any high stakes situations, so are less likely to be considered a problem. Other uses of English in Sweden described below have, however, come under discussion, as they affect high stakes domains and situations.

## English in education

In Swedish education, Swedish is the main language used, but English is strongly present at certain levels. At the primary and secondary levels, the majority of schools have Swedish as a medium of instruction and English is a subject that all students need to study, but English as a medium of instruction (EMI) is not that common. There are some schools where pupils can take the International Baccalaureate programme and a number of schools provide education through Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL). Some of these are International English Schools, which tend to have many pupils and which are located in big cities: Three of the 10 largest primary schools in Sweden are International English Schools, for example. In comparison to other countries, however, in total not that many children learn through English. Very few primary schools offer CLIL; so only about 1% of primary school learners learn through CLIL (Skolverket, 2010) . At the secondary level, more pupils learn through CLIL, although it is difficult to know exactly how many: Studies have estimated the proportion of Swedish secondary schools offering CLIL to be from as low as 4% (Skolverket, 2018) to as high as 33% (Yoxsimer Paulsrud, 2014) .

More so than the primary and secondary education, Swedish higher education (HE) is where English is in use the most. Malmström and Pecorari's (2022) survey of English in research and higher education has shown that today the use of English in Swedish universities is widespread, although there are some differences between the type of education (course vs. programme), level (undergraduate vs. master's) and discipline (national vs. international focus). While at the undergraduate level the proportion of EMI is more modest (18% of courses, 4% of programmes), at the master's level the majority of courses (53%) and programmes (64%) are given in English. Almost half of the students in EMI programmes are local students (Wächter & Maiworm, 2014) , but in courses the proportion is probably even higher, which means that many Swedish students study through English.

At the disciplinary level, fewer master's courses are given in English in disciplines where the focus or relevance is more likely to be national or local, but a majority of courses are in English in those disciplines where the focus is international (see Table 1 ). Thus, only a quarter of master's courses in medicine are in English, as students will likely be local practitioners, but the proportion is slightly higher in the humanities and even more so in the social sciences,

where the focus of study is often not local. However, a large majority of master's courses in the natural sciences and engineering are in English. Of course, there is also variation within the disciplines themselves, and how much EMI there is will depend on the subdiscipline and subject area. Salö and Josephson (2014) have reported that in history, for example, the majority of teaching is in Swedish at both levels, while in psychology, linguistics and law, undergraduate teaching is typically Swedish, but the language of master's education depends on the university or subdiscipline and focus. Physics and computer science, on the other hand, have a majority of undergraduate teaching in Swedish, but at the master's level the teaching is in English only, as is the case in the natural sciences in general. In some subjects, then, English has made great inroads.

The picture is even more complex, however, once we consider that even Swedish-medium courses often include English components. A majority (65%) of the undergraduate courses surveyed by Malmström and Pecorari (2022) had at least some assigned reading in English. There are only moderate differences between disciplines (Table 1 ): the smallest proportion of assigned reading in English was found in medicine (roughly 30%) and the highest in the social sciences and natural sciences (roughly 50%). The differences in proportions between the disciplines are therefore not that great. On top of this, in some Swedish-medium courses, students are given the option of writing assignments in English (Gunnarsson, 2001) , they do a number of labs in English or attend Swedish lectures where the presentation slides are in English (Bolton & Kuteeva, 2012) . There is also anecdotal evidence that some lecturers switch to English if they feel the need for it. This is supported by the fact that some course descriptions found on university websites include phrases such as 'English on request' . Most Swedish students are therefore very likely to have at least a part of or an aspect of their higher education in English.
